name: Peg-MGF (mechano growth factor)

lead: Peg-MGF is used by some bodybuilders hoping for extra muscle growth and a bigger, fuller physique after training. It is sold online as a research chemical.

Mechano growth factor (IGF-1Ec) is a 24-amino-acid peptide the body makes from the IGF-1 gene during muscle repair after exercise. Natural MGF is rapidly degraded, and pegylation in the synthetic form is intended to improve stability. Published work is laboratory and animal research on muscle repair, aging and neuroprotection, and reference sources report no human clinical trial results for MGF as a muscle-building drug.

paras: Users take it as a post-training peptide, often alongside other muscle-building compounds. It is bought as a research product and is not a medicine; there is no established protocol.
Not approved as a medicine anywhere, and human safety data are not available. The World Anti-Doping Agency prohibits MGF, and a 2020 review raised concerns about potential carcinogenicity.

angle.text: Sold as a research chemical that bodybuilders take after training in hopes of extra muscle growth and a fuller physique. The idea draws on MGF's role in muscle repair; work so far is cell and animal research, and the compound is WADA-banned.

lead: Mechano growth factor (MGF), also called IGF-1Ec, is a naturally occurring 24-amino-acid peptide produced from the IGF-1 gene during muscle repair after exercise, and is described as having anabolic effects.[1] PEG-MGF is a pegylated synthetic form sold as a research chemical.[1]

Research on MGF is mainly laboratory and animal work covering muscle repair and aging, signaling in muscle growth, neuroprotection and cardiac protection, and reviews have questioned its role in repair.[1] No human clinical trial results are reported in the reference article, which also notes the World Anti-Doping Agency has banned MGF and that a 2020 review raised concerns about potential carcinogenicity.[1]

paras: MGF is the C-terminal fragment associated with the IGF-1Ec splice variant and is produced in muscle after loading or damage.[1] Natural MGF is broken down quickly in the body, and synthetic versions often incorporate unnatural D-amino acids in the central region for metabolic stability, and in some products the tyrosine is pegylated.[1]

Cited studies address muscle repair and aging, signaling pathways in muscle growth, neuroprotection after brain ischemia, protection of heart tissue after infarction, neurogenesis in aging mouse brains and nerve regeneration.[1] These are laboratory and animal findings. Reviews by some authors have questioned MGF's role in repair, and a 2020 review raised concern about possible carcinogenicity.[1]

MGF's anabolic reputation has led to illicit use by athletes, and the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibits it; doping-control detection methods were published in 2009, 2014 and 2017.[1] In bodybuilding communities, Peg-MGF is sold and discussed as a research peptide, often alongside growth hormone or IGF-1 related products.

No studies found. Research on MGF is limited to laboratory and animal work. A registered trial of a different long-acting growth hormone product, pegylated somatropin, in short-stature children is unrelated to Peg-MGF.[2]
